turn_text: Consumer brief prices were up four and a half percent last month. Ranchers, Calcalf producers, as I understand, they're not seeing any additional dollars at this point. What have we learned about the imbalance and what are your concerns or suggestions here?

We need more competition in the marketplace. Capitalism doesn't work when you have consolidation, and that's what we have in the meat industry right now. And everybody needs to make a profit. And what we're seeing right now is the Packers are making a real profit. Our cap folks are going broke, and our small and medium sized feeders are going broke. I talked about the food chain a second ago as it applied to the drought. If we don't do something at the federal level, this is going to be bad, really bad, for our food chain. These folks go broke. It's going to change the look of this country, and it's going to change food security in this country forever. So what needs to happen? We need to address the issue of consolidation. This is not a new problem. It's been around, you know, for 30, 40, 50 years. And right now, we've got four companies that control 80% of the meat in this country. That's not competition. That's the four people going on in a golf course and figuring out what they're going to pay and what they're going to charge, the consumer. And so we've got a bill that was passed over a hundred years ago called the Packers and Stockyard Act. It is never, I shouldn't say never, but let's put it this way. It could have more teeth in it. And so Senator Grassley There's been around here for a long time and myself have dropped in a bill to put a special investigator in the Department of Agriculture that have investigatory powers and subpoena powers to be able to put some teeth into the Packers and Stockyards Act so that if there is collusion and there is price fixing, that these folks can be held accountable. In the meantime, we're working with Secretary Vilsack. He announced yesterday he's got about 500 billion dollars that they're going to put out there for loans, at least a portion of that for loans, for startup and expanding existing meat processing. What will that do? That'll let a small meat processing plant in Montana or any other state be able to expand and address and be competitive with the big boys. And that'll put more competition in the marketplace. And I think it'll end up with a fairer market. and more competition. I've also got some stuff that I'm doing all the stuff with Drassley. He's been a leader on this and has a buy on these issues for him longer than I have because he's been here a lot longer than I am. But we've also got another one that sets a cash price of cattle at 50%. Right now it's 10% or 12%. And when it's that low, those cash prices can be manipulated to deal with the formula pricing and drive those prices down. Bottom line is this. We've got a problem and we need to address it. It's a problem that has been around for a long time. I think we're starting to see people on both sides of the aisle take notice of this. So if we can get a bipartisan push to get some of these things done, I think it can make a big difference to the bottom line of our cow-calf producers and our small and medium-sized feeders be allowed to stay in business and make an honest living. and have a fair market. And that's really where it's at. And we've got to fix this. If we don't fix this and we don't fix it soon, I'm going to tell you, our food security is not going to be where we need it to be in this country. And I'm passionate about this because I've seen many of my friends and neighbors go broke, not because they're bad operators, because they were in a system that was rigged for the Packers. And we need to make sure that that rig in stops.
